content: Who can find a worthy woman? For her value is far above rubies. {{v:11}} The heart of her husband trusts in her. He shall have no lack of gain. {{v:12}} She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. {{v:13}} She seeks wool and flax, and works eagerly with her hands. {{v:14}} She is like the merchant ships. She brings her bread from afar. {{v:15}} She rises also while it is yet night, gives food to her household, and portions for her servant girls. {{v:16}} She considers a field, and buys it. With the fruit of her hands, she plants a vineyard. {{v:17}} She arms her waist with strength, and makes her arms strong. {{v:18}} She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp doesn’t go out by night. {{v:19}} She lays her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. {{v:20}} She opens her arms to the poor; yes, she extends her hands to the needy. {{v:21}} She is not afraid of the snow for her household, for all her household are clothed with scarlet. {{v:22}} She makes for herself carpets of tapestry. Her clothing is fine linen and purple. {{v:23}} Her husband is respected in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land. {{v:24}} She makes linen garments and sells them, and delivers sashes to the merchant. {{v:25}} Strength and dignity are her clothing. She laughs at the time to come. {{v:26}} She opens her mouth with wisdom. Kind instruction is on her tongue. {{v:27}} She looks well to the ways of her household, and doesn’t eat the bread of idleness. {{v:28}} Her children rise up and call her blessed. Her husband also praises her: {{v:29}} “Many women do noble things, but you excel them all.” {{v:30}} Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised. {{v:31}} Give her of the fruit of her hands! Let her works praise her in the gates!

facets.text: The poem's climactic verse locates the woman's true worth not in charm or beauty, which it dismisses as deceptive and fleeting, but in the fear of the LORD. This is the same fear of the LORD that Proverbs names as the beginning of wisdom (Prov 1:7; 9:10), so the whole acrostic portrait functions as the book's crowning embodiment of wisdom incarnate in a human life. Her many virtues flow from and point back to this single reverent orientation toward God.
facets.question: What is the real source of a person's worth according to Proverbs 31?

facets.text: The passage praises the woman not for passive virtue but for tireless, competent labor: she trades, plants a vineyard, manages servants, and profits from her merchandise. Scripture here dignifies ordinary economic work, industry, and stewardship of resources as genuine expressions of righteousness and wisdom. The condemnation of 'the bread of idleness' reinforces that diligence itself is a moral and spiritual good.
facets.question: How does Scripture regard hard work and industry as part of a virtuous life?

facets.text: Amid her many enterprises the woman deliberately opens her hands to the poor and extends them to the needy. Her productivity is not self-serving accumulation but overflows into generosity, showing that authentic wisdom bears fruit in care for the vulnerable. This anticipates the biblical conviction that love of God is inseparable from active mercy toward the poor.
facets.question: How is caring for the poor connected to a life of wisdom?

facets.text: The woman speaks with wisdom, and 'kind instruction is on her tongue,' making her a teacher within her household as well as its provider. Strength and dignity clothe her, and she 'laughs at the time to come,' displaying a fearless confidence rooted in her trust in God. The passage thus honors feminine wisdom as authoritative, courageous, and formative for the whole family.
facets.question: What does Proverbs teach about a woman's wisdom and confidence in facing the future?

facets.text: Catholic tradition has read this 'worthy woman' typologically as a figure of the Church, the Bride of Christ, and of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose works praise her in the gates of heaven. The trusting husband foreshadows Christ who entrusts himself to his Bride, and her ceaseless labor images the Church's fruitful charity across the ages. This spiritual reading fittingly places the poem in the liturgy's honoring of holy women and of Our Lady.
facets.question: How does the Church read the worthy woman of Proverbs 31 as a figure of Mary or the Church?

facets.text: The passage closes by insisting that the woman's own works praise her in the gates and that she be given the fruit of her hands, placing her righteous deeds on public display where the elders sit. This affirms that a life of faithful labor and reverence merits genuine recognition, and that good works are the visible testimony of an interior fear of the LORD. Her reward is not vanity but the just acknowledgment her deeds have earned.
facets.question: Why does Proverbs say a person's works themselves should be their praise?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The acrostic poem of the "worthy woman" crowns Proverbs by portraying practical wisdom incarnate in a life of industry, generosity, and instruction, all rooted in the fear of the LORD; Catholic tradition reads it typologically of Mary and the Church.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: True worth lies not in fleeting charm or beauty but in the fear of the LORD, the beginning of wisdom, which crowns and unifies the whole portrait.
[MORAL | traditional]: Scripture dignifies diligent labor, trade, and stewardship as expressions of righteousness, condemning idleness as a moral failing.
[MORAL | explicit]: The woman's productivity overflows into generosity toward the poor and needy, showing wisdom bears fruit in active mercy.
[MORAL | traditional]: Her wise speech, kind instruction, strength, dignity, and fearless confidence honor feminine wisdom as authoritative and formative for the household.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The Church reads the worthy woman as a figure of the Bride of Christ, the Church, and the Blessed Virgin Mary, with the trusting husband foreshadowing Christ.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: Her works themselves praise her in the gates, affirming that faithful deeds are the just and public testimony of an interior fear of the LORD.

content: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven: {{v:2}} a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; {{v:3}} a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; {{v:4}} a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; {{v:5}} a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; {{v:6}} a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; {{v:7}} a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; {{v:8}} a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

facets.text: The famous refrain 'a time for every purpose under heaven' teaches that human life unfolds within an ordered rhythm of seasons that God has appointed. Nothing in the created order is random; birth and death, planting and uprooting, all have their proper moment within a divinely governed time. This poetic catalogue insists that wisdom consists not in mastering time but in recognizing and receiving the season God gives.
facets.question: Does everything in life happen at an appointed time?

facets.text: By pairing each activity with its opposite—weeping and laughing, keeping and casting away, war and peace—the poem embraces the full range of human experience without denying its contradictions. It refuses to pretend that life is only joyful or only sorrowful; both the tearing and the sewing belong to the fabric of existence. This honesty about life's polarities is itself a form of wisdom that neither despairs nor evades reality.
facets.question: Why does life contain both joy and sorrow, building up and breaking down?

facets.text: The Preacher's insistence that even killing, breaking down, and hating have 'a time' does not license human autonomy over these acts but confesses the limits of human comprehension before God's providence. The Qoheleth's larger argument is that man cannot grasp the whole 'work that God has done from the beginning to the end' (3:11); the seasons are God's to appoint, not ours to command. The passage thus fosters humility and trust rather than fatalism.
facets.question: Does this poem justify human control over life and death, or does it teach humility before God?

facets.text: The list moves through the whole span from birth to death, encompassing labor, emotion, relationship, speech, and even the making of peace and war, presenting human life as a totality held within God's timing. This wholeness anticipates the Wisdom tradition's conviction that a life lived in the fear of the Lord finds its meaning not in any single season but in surrendering the whole to God. The believer is invited to sanctify each moment as it comes rather than clinging to one season against another.
facets.question: How should a believer respond to the changing seasons of life?

facets.text: Read in the light of Christ, the appointed 'times' find their fulfillment in the fullness of time when God sent his Son (Galatians 4:4), and in Jesus' own repeated awareness that his 'hour' had come. What Ecclesiastes glimpses as an inscrutable rhythm under heaven the Gospel reveals as the unfolding of God's saving plan, so that every season is gathered up into the mystery of redemption. The Christian therefore reads these paired times as pointing toward the One who is Lord of time and eternity.
facets.question: How does Christ fulfill the mysterious 'times and seasons' of Ecclesiastes?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 presents its famous poem of paired 'times,' teaching that all of human life unfolds within a divinely ordered rhythm of seasons; Catholic reflection reads it as wisdom about providence, human humility, and ultimately Christ as Lord of time.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Life unfolds within an ordered rhythm of appointed seasons under God's governance; nothing is random, and wisdom means receiving the season God gives.
[PHILOSOPHICAL | traditional]: The poem's opposing pairs embrace life's full range of joy and sorrow, honestly holding its contradictions without despair or evasion.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: Even the harsh 'times' confess the limits of human understanding before God's providence, fostering humility and trust rather than fatalism or autonomy over life and death.
[MORAL | inferential]: Presenting life as a totality held within God's timing, the passage invites the believer to sanctify each moment and surrender the whole life to God rather than clinging to one season.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: Read in Christ, the appointed times are fulfilled in the fullness of time (Gal 4:4) and Jesus' awareness of his 'hour,' revealing every season as part of God's saving plan under the Lord of time.
